lesson_title: The Country's Till Slip: C, G, I and the Big Three Aggregates
hook_text: A whole country's shopping on one till slip — and one item on it is in the wrong pile.
clip_script: Imagine the entire country doing one year's shopping, and every purchase lands on one giant till slip. Sort it into piles and you have just built the national accounts. Biggest pile: households. Groceries, taxi fares, school fees, airtime, a fridge. That's C — about three rand in every five. Sort it by how long things last: the fridge lasts years, the shoes last a while, the bread is gone by Thursday, and the taxi ride leaves nothing at all. Handy fact — when money gets tight nobody stops eating, but everybody postpones the couch. That's why furniture shops feel a downturn before spaza shops do. Second pile: government's day-to-day shopping — paying the nurse, buying the chalk, keeping the clinic lights on. That's G. Now the trap. The social grant your neighbour gets is NOT in that pile. Government bought nothing with it. It gets counted later, when your neighbour buys maize meal. Count it twice and the country looks richer than it is. Third pile, and the important one: the bakkie, the road, the power station, the orchard. Things still there next year, doing work. That's investment — the only pile that makes next year bigger.
visual_style: One long paper till slip unspooling down the screen, items flying off it into three glowing labelled piles; a grant slip bouncing out of the government pile and landing in the household pile.
pacing: Fast sorting rhythm, one hard stop at the grant trap, expansive close on the third pile.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and run GVA to GDP to GNI in both directions.
